analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act in its entirety and restores the law as it stood before 2010.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the Affordable Care Act was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a vote or a hearing.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase the Affordable Care Act — the 2010 law that created the insurance marketplaces, expanded Medicaid, protected people with pre-existing conditions, allowed young adults to stay on their parents' insurance, and set minimum standards for what health plans must cover. It would also erase the companion 2010 law that adjusted the ACA's subsidies and tax provisions. Everything the ACA changed would snap back to the law as it existed before 2010. The bill contained no replacement provisions.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be higher-income taxpayers and health-related industries that paid ACA taxes and fees, since the repeal restores the pre-2010 tax rules. Insurers, drug makers, and device makers would be freed from ACA fees and coverage requirements. People who were healthier, higher-income, or uninsured by choice would gain from the end of the individual mandate and the removal of plan rules, while the roughly tens of millions who had gained coverage or protections under the law would lose them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, insurers, and medical industries

how_it_helps.text: It would erase the Affordable Care Act's rules on insurers, which supporters argued raised premiums and limited consumer choice of plans.
It would also erase the law's taxes and penalties, including the individual mandate penalty and ACA-related tax increases on higher incomes and industry, restoring the pre-2010 tax rules.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would fall on people with pre-existing conditions, who could again be denied coverage or charged more; low- and middle-income people who received premium subsidies or had gained Medicaid coverage; young adults who could stay on a parent's plan; and seniors and others who benefited from ACA provisions like reduced drug costs in Medicare.
analysis.who_pays_short: People with pre-existing conditions and subsidized coverage

drawbacks.text: Repealing the ACA would end its insurance protections, including the ban on denying or charging more for pre-existing conditions, the ability of young adults to stay on a parent's plan, and the requirement that plans cover essential health benefits.
The repeal would eliminate premium subsidies and the Medicaid expansion, which by 2013 had begun extending coverage to lower-income Americans, without any replacement provisions in the bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the millions who gained coverage, protections, or subsidies under the ACA, the bill's cost — losing all of that with no stated replacement — outweighed any benefit from lower regulatory burdens and premiums for healthier, higher-income people who did not benefit from the law. The bill offered nothing for people with pre-existing conditions or subsidized coverage, making its drawbacks severe.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and sat there until the Congress ended, with no vote or hearing.

narrative.text: Senator David Vitter, joined by Senator Ted Cruz, introduced S. 499 on March 7, 2013 to repeal the Affordable Care Act and the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; no further action appears in the record.
The 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 with the bill still in committee, so it never received a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the Affordable Care Act's coverage expansions and insurance rules stayed in place, and the industries and higher-income taxpayers that would have benefited from its taxes being repealed gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nothing changed; the ACA stayed in place

for.name: Sen. David Vitter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Affordable Care Act and its companion reconciliation act.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only Republican support — a single Republican cosponsor besides its sponsor — and no Democratic support appears in the record.

industries.note: Repeal would free insurers from ACA rules on what plans must cover, guaranteed issue, and rate review, but also end the subsidized customer base and mandate that brought insurers millions of new paying customers. The bill restores the pre-2010 insurance market.

industries.industry: Medical device makers, drug companies, and high-income taxpayers
industries.note: The ACA imposed industry fees and higher taxes on upper incomes to fund coverage expansion; repeal removes those costs. Those gains come at the expense of the coverage expansion the taxes financed.
Hospitals accepted ACA payment cuts in exchange for coverage expansion that reduced uncompensated care; repeal without replacement would restore the cuts while removing the coverage.
